claims.text: Enhanced Monte Carlo sampling methods can quantify nucleation barriers.
Monte Carlo-derived nucleation barriers can be used to design thermal processing routes that control phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
The relevant Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy initially contains multiple constituent phases.
Advanced Monte Carlo sampling can map the free-energy landscape under varied thermal histories.
Annealing temperature, dwell time, and cooling rate can be selected from predicted nucleation barriers.
Systematic variation of annealing temperature, holding time, and cooling rate can drive selective nucleation and growth of desired phases.
Nucleation barriers control the onset and evolution of transformations between constituent phases.
Enhanced sampling can quantify phase free-energy differences and associated nucleation barriers under different thermal conditions.
Quantified free energies and nucleation barriers identify processing windows that preferentially form or suppress particular phases.
Monte Carlo-informed thermal processing will produce a more controlled and reproducible phase distribution than standard heat treatment.
The controlled phase distribution will improve mechanical strength or thermal stability.
Conventional heat treatments produce uncontrolled or suboptimal phase distributions in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
The method is expected to work when thermal history dominates the phase transformations.
Compositional inhomogeneity and kinetic limitations not represented by the simulation may reduce the method's effectiveness.
Quantitative phase-fraction and performance improvements depend on calibration between Monte Carlo predictions and real thermal dynamics.
Microstructural defects and local composition variations may affect the resulting phases and performance.
XRD, TEM, and DSC measurements can compare phase distributions and transformation behavior between conventional and Monte Carlo-informed treatments.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant, reproducible phase-distribution difference or correlation with predicted barriers would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The baseline characterizes conventional heat treatment as producing uncontrolled or suboptimal phase distributions, while the predicted-outcome wording can be read as saying that standard heat treatments are where phase fractions are more uniformly and reproducibly tuned.
